surface_forms: la dame à coiffure blanche à la Marie-Antoinette
la dame coiffée à la Marie-Antoinette

appraisal_events.evidence: the narrator calls Villeparisis and her two peers 'trois divinités déchues' whose supposedly exclusive salons actually receive only 'la lie de gens dont on ne voulait pas ailleurs'; Villeparisis pointedly avoids introducing Bloch to Alix in retaliation ('un rendu') for Alix having secretly poached Mme Ristori from her the day before, and Alix's glacial snub of the narrator is unmasked as compensatory hauteur born of 'une disgrâce particulière.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's ironic exposition strips away the pretension of grandeur from both Villeparisis and Alix, showing their real social decline, mutual pettiness, and performed hauteur as symptoms of fallen status rather than genuine eminence.

appraisal_events.evidence: Alix implies the Louvre portrait is the copy, citing Liszt's supposed remark and her own role in bringing him; Villeparisis dismisses this ('il était déjà gâteux et je ne me rappelle pas qu'il ait jamais dit cela'), denies Alix introduced her to Liszt, and trumps her with 'j'avais dîné vingt fois avec lui chez la princesse de Sayn-Wittgenstein.'
appraisal_events.explanation: In this closing exchange Villeparisis firmly rebuts Alix's implied dig and counters with a stronger personal claim of intimacy with Liszt, coming out locally ahead in the rivalry, while Alix's gambit is deflated.

status_effects.explanation: She is framed as one of the 'fallen goddesses,' her salon's real exclusivity undercut and her private pettiness toward Alix exposed.
She wins the closing verbal exchange with Alix, dismissing her claim and asserting superior personal acquaintance with Liszt.
Alix is likewise exposed as a declined society figure whose icy hauteur toward the narrator is revealed as compensatory rather than a mark of real standing.
Her insinuation about the portrait and her claimed closeness to Liszt are both rebuffed and outdone by Villeparisis in the exchange.

ambiguities: The old lady addressed as 'Alix' by Mme de Villeparisis is not matched to any reference-sheet entity; within this passage she is treated as an unresolved distinct character, one of the 'trois divinités déchues' introduced in the prior context.

Villeparisis's advantage in the closing Liszt/portrait exchange is inferred from the sequencing and confidence of her reply rather than from explicit narratorial comment, so the narrative stance is read as neutral report rather than clearly endorsed.
